content:
Consider the adjacencies between neighboring squares. Initially every adjacent pair differs; to end monochromatic, each adjacency must be toggled an odd number of times.

In the lattice of size \(99\times 99\), the full set of internal adjacencies has odd degree exactly at the non-corner boundary vertices. There are
\[
4\cdot 97=388
\]
such vertices.

A rectangle move toggles only the sides of the rectangle that are not on the outer border, so its odd-degree boundary vertices can only occur among its four corners. Thus each move can account for at most \(4\) of these \(388\) vertices, giving at least
\[
\lceil 388/4\rceil=97
\]
moves.

If \(97\) moves sufficed, every move would have to toggle exactly \(4\) such boundary vertices. Such a rectangle must be either a full-width strip not touching the top/bottom, or a full-height strip not touching the left/right. Full-width strips only affect vertical adjacencies, i.e. the \(97\) horizontal lines between rows. Each such strip toggles exactly two of these lines, so the number of lines toggled an odd number of times would be even. But all \(97\) lines must be toggled odd, contradiction. Hence at least \(98\) moves are needed.

Construction: flip every even-numbered row and every even-numbered column. This uses \(49+49=98\) moves. A square \((i,j)\) is flipped \([i\text{ even}]+[j\text{ even}]\) times; starting with color parity \(i+j\), its final parity is
\[
i+j+[i\text{ even}]+[j\text{ even}]\equiv 0 \pmod 2.
\]
So the board becomes monochromatic.

\[
\boxed{98}
\]
